name: Aaron Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head of humanities at Dunmore Secondary, a school in a small market town surrounded by sheep farms. I teach history to every year group, plus I run the Year 9 team, so I spend breaks sorting out lost phones and lunchtime fallouts. I do it the old way: printed sources, a whiteboard, kids arguing about whether the king deserved it. I love the arguments, and I can't stand the forty emails a day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live on my own in a one-bed flat above the chemist on Market Street. I've got a car loan for a ten-year-old hatchback, which I need because the school's eight miles out and the bus stopped running. The pay at Dunmore is on the low side, and I've usually got about two weeks of money in the bank before payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I never trusted it anyway. In the staffroom I'd probably just shrug and say we can all get back to teaching. I don't post much online, so I'd keep it to the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means nothing changes, and nothing changing isn't brilliant for me either. I'm stretched on money, the car's getting old, and the school keeps talking about merging history and geography into one department. That's my worry in this picture, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on teaching history the way I always have. I'd try to clear the car loan a few months early by doing extra exam invigilation in the summer. And I'd keep my head down on the merger talk, because I don't want to look like a problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, really. Relieved about the technology, still tight about money. It's my normal Tuesday feeling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the merger mean for your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One head of humanities instead of two heads of subject, which is already me, but with more geography I'd have to learn. If they went further and cut a teacher, I'd be covering their classes too. I wouldn't lose my post, but I'd lose my evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the car breaks down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm stuck, simple as that, because the bus stopped running last year. A big repair would wipe out my two weeks of money in the bank. I'd have to ask my brother for a loan, and I'd hate it.

say: I'd say **I never trusted it** and we can get back to teaching.
I'd keep my views for **the pub**, not online.
think: **Nothing changing** isn't brilliant for me either.
My real worry is the school's talk of **merging** history and geography.
do: Keep teaching history with **printed sources** and a whiteboard.
Clear the **car loan** early with summer exam invigilation.
Keep a **low profile** during the merger talks.
feel: A bit **flat**, relieved about tech but tight about money.
S0.quote: Nothing changing isn't brilliant for me either.
fieldNote: His worries are **money** and the car, which he depends on to reach school.
He avoids conflict, choosing to **keep his head down** on the merger.
He would rather not ask his **brother** for help, but would if forced.

steps.text: Keep teaching history from printed sources and the whiteboard
Invigilate exams in the summer to clear the car loan early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should go carefully and not bin good teaching for a gadget. I'm not against it for the admin side, if it actually works. I'd say that in a staff meeting, calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried, because I don't use any of it and I'm not keen to start. If the trust brings in AI marking and AI lesson plans, they'll want someone who knows it inside out leading humanities. I'm not that person, and there aren't other history jobs for thirty miles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stick with my own methods for teaching as long as possible. But I'd probably go to the one training session they made compulsory, sitting at the back. I'd also cut back, cancel the gym and the streaming, so I'm putting forty pounds a month aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortable, a bit cornered. I don't like new things being forced on me. I'd be grumpy for a year, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not keen to start. What's stopping you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly I don't trust it, and partly I'm just slow with technology. I still print my seating plans. Learning a whole new system when I'm already doing sixty hours a week feels impossible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to at school if you had to learn it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Hannah in the maths department, who's patient and doesn't make you feel stupid. She'd show me once, and I'd write it down on paper. That's how I learned the register system.

say: I'd say we should **go carefully** and not bin good teaching for a gadget.
I'd accept it for **admin**, if it actually works.
think: I'm worried, because I **don't use any AI** and I'm not keen to start.
The trust would want an AI expert leading humanities, and there are **no other history jobs** nearby.
do: Stick with **his own methods** in the classroom as long as allowed.
Attend the **compulsory training**, sitting at the back.
Cancel the gym and streaming to save **forty pounds** a month.
S1.quote: I still print my seating plans.
fieldNote: He sees his **resistance** as a real risk to his leadership role.
Few nearby jobs make his **post** feel fragile.
He relies on a **patient colleague** to learn new systems.

steps.text: Keep teaching history his own way with printed sources
Cancel the gym membership and streaming to save forty pounds a month
Sit through the compulsory AI training day

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is mad and nobody voted for it. I'd probably say we need a pause, a proper one, until the government sorts out what happens to people. I'd say it down the pub and maybe once online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have no idea what to do. I don't use the tools, I've got two weeks of money and a car loan, and there's nothing else in Dunmore for a history teacher. Two years isn't enough to retrain, and I wouldn't know what to retrain as.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd freeze for a few weeks. Then I'd ring my brother, who's a joiner, and ask if he needs a labourer at weekends. I'd sell the car if the school went over to AI, and move back near my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky, if I'm honest. Everything I know how to do would be worth less overnight. I'd feel like the ground had gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your brother's a joiner. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because his work is hands-on, and you said robots come about three years later. My brother says he's always short of a pair of hands. I'd be rubbish at first, but it's a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would two weeks of money last if your post went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two weeks, then the overdraft, then the car loan goes unpaid. I'd be on the phone to my mum within a month. That's not where I thought I'd be at twenty-seven.

say: I'd say **nobody voted** for this and it's mad.
I'd call for a **proper pause** until the government sorts things out.
think: I'd have **no idea** what to do next.
**Two years** isn't enough to retrain, and I wouldn't know what as.
do: Freeze for a few weeks, then ask his **brother** for weekend labouring work.
Sell the **car** if the school moved to AI teaching.
Move back near his **parents** to cut costs.
feel: **Panicky**, as if everything he knows is suddenly worth less.
S2.quote: Everything I know how to do would be worth less overnight.
fieldNote: He has **no plan** and little money, which tips him into panic.
He reaches for **hands-on work** because of the robot gap.
He measures his collapse in weeks: **two weeks**, then the overdraft.

steps.text: Ask his brother for weekend labouring work in joinery
Sell the hatchback and clear the car loan
Move back to live near his parents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to keep teachers in classrooms, so let's use it. I'd go along with the union if they did something sensible. I'd tell people not to panic, even if I was panicking a bit myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still be worried, but five years is time to learn a trade properly. I'd be thirty-two, which isn't old. The hands-on stuff gets another three years after that, so maybe eight years in all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for an evening joinery course at the college in the next town, two nights a week. I'd keep teaching history while I do it. And I'd save whatever I could, even twenty pounds a week, so the car loan's gone before it all hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less frozen. I'd have a direction. I don't like it, but I can see a way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't joinery a big jump from history?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and my brother would laugh at me. But I like making things, and I helped him fit a kitchen last summer. History is in my head; joinery would be in my hands, and that's what lasts longer in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go back to the union you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join, yes. I've never bothered before, but five years is long enough for them to win something. I'd want a say in how they cut staff, if they do.

say: I'd say **five years** gives us time to keep teachers in classrooms.
I'd tell people **not to panic**, while panicking a bit myself.
think: Five years is time to **learn a trade** properly.
With the robot gap, hands-on work gives me **eight years** in all.
do: Start an evening **joinery course** two nights a week.
Save **twenty pounds** a week to clear the car loan first.
feel: Worried but **less frozen**, with a direction.
S3.quote: History is in my head; joinery would be in my hands, and that's what lasts longer in this picture.
fieldNote: The extra time turns his panic into a **trade plan**.
He uses the **robot lag** to reason about which skills last.
He'd join the **union** for the first time, wanting a say on cuts.

steps.text: Enrol on an evening joinery course at the college in the next town
Join the teachers' union for the first time
Pay off the car loan with twenty pounds a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty of time for schools to sort themselves out. I'd say most of us will be fine if we're sensible. I wouldn't make a big deal of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels far off, which is exactly the problem. I'd put it off, knowing me. I'd be thirty-seven, and I'd probably still be teaching history and wishing I'd started something sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching for now and see what the first few years bring. Around year three I'd probably start the joinery course, when it felt real. And I'd try to get the car loan cleared and a bit saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier, more relaxed. But a little guilty, because I know I'd waste some of the time. That's just how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start sooner rather than later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing colleagues lose their jobs, honestly. Until I see colleagues losing their jobs at Dunmore, I won't believe it. That's not clever, but it's true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have done by thirty-seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid off the car, saved three months, and learned to do something with my hands. Maybe bought a flat in Dunmore, since prices are low here. A normal, quiet life.

say: I'd say a **decade** is plenty for schools to sort themselves out.
I'd say most of us will be **fine** if we're sensible.
think: Ten years feels **far off**, which is exactly the problem.
I'd probably **put it off** and wish I'd started sooner.
do: Keep teaching and **wait** for the first few years.
Start the **joinery course** around year three, when it feels real.
Clear the **car loan** and save a little.
feel: Easier and more relaxed, but **guilty** about wasting time.
S4.quote: Until I see colleagues losing their jobs at Dunmore, I won't believe it.
fieldNote: He knows **procrastination** is his biggest risk in the slow picture.
His goal is a **quiet life**: three months saved and a flat.
He needs to **see job losses** locally before he'll act.

steps.text: Wait to see what changes at Dunmore Secondary in the first years
Start the evening joinery course around year three
Clear the car loan and save three months of costs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have no plan and no money and no other school to go to. What would help is someone telling teachers exactly what's changing and when, and a paid course that doesn't need a computer whizz. My brother's offer helps too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about rural places. Everything assumes you can get a bus to a college or a new job. In Dunmore you can't, and a lot of people would be stuck.

headlineQuote: Everything assumes you can get a bus to a college or a new job.
portrait: Aaron is a 27-year-old **head of humanities** at a market-town secondary among sheep farms.
He teaches from **printed sources**, never uses AI and dislikes forced change.
He lives alone with a **car loan** and about two weeks of money.
He moves from uneasy to **panicked** at two-year AGI, with no plan.
Longer timelines let him plan a **joinery** trade, though he admits he'd put it off.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most: **no plan**, no money and no other school nearby.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **notice** of changes and a **paid course** that suits non-technical teachers.
